changes.old_value: Every causal claim harbors a hidden counterfactual. When we say 'the assassination caused the war,' we implicitly assert 'had there been no assassination, there would have been no war.' This counterfactual backbone is the skeleton of causation itself—yet it remains largely invisible to both authors and readers. The problem is not merely academic: policy debates hinge on counterfactual claims ('sanctions would have worked'), historical judgments rest on them ('appeasement caused the war'), and mo...
changes.new_value: A one-page audit of the text’s consequential suppositions: antecedent and owner, fixed background and extra changes, bridge and modal force, relevant alternative, and what independently survives. Desks lift scenarios, dependencies and robustness tables. A genuine inferential counterexample qualifies without literal if–then syntax. A text advancing a what-if or counterexample, with historical background only where its kind of claim requires it.
